title: The Jerusalem Talmud
hook: sages in Galilee complete a Talmud, the teaching of the land itself

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah: three answers about the evening Shema, and Gamaliel's sons home late from a wedding. Your line was the oral, written. Did you mention someone else's way of doing something? Day nine hundred eight.

One star in the sky: it's still day. Two stars: nobody's sure. Three stars: now it's night. That little rule of thumb comes from a conversation about yesterday's question, when the evening Shema may begin. The Mishnah said the time starts when the priests go in to eat their holy portion. But what does that look like if you're standing outside, with no priest in sight? You look up and count. The conversation that counts the stars was carried on by sages who lived in the land of Israel itself, in towns around the Galilee. What they built is known by a name that points somewhere else entirely.
screen: `ONE STAR: DAY.` → `TWO STARS: UNSURE.` → `THREE STARS: NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Once the Mishnah was written, students did what students do. They asked questions of it. Why does this teacher say midnight? What's the source in the Torah? What if the case is a little different? Their long, recorded discussion of the Mishnah is called Gemara, and Mishnah plus Gemara together is a Talmud. There are two. The one we meet today is usually called the Jerusalem Talmud, in Hebrew the Yerushalmi. But its sages taught in the Galilee, not in Jerusalem. Its older names say where it came from: the Talmud of the Land of Israel, the Talmud of the West. That's today's line: the land's talmud. You can feel the land in it. It has Gemara on the order of Seeds, the farming laws: tithes, the corner of the field left for the poor, the seventh year when the land rests. These are laws tied to the soil of the land, and here they are discussed by sages who lived on it. Its language is close to the Aramaic spoken around them. Some readers notice something else. The Yerushalmi can be terse. Arguments start and stop. A question is raised and the page moves on. Some readers sense a work that was never fully smoothed out. Students still learn it, unfinished edges and all, reading closely what is there.
screen: `MISHNAH PLUS GEMARA IS A TALMUD.` · `NAMED FOR JERUSALEM, MADE IN GALILEE.` · then, large: `THE TALMUD OF THE LAND OF ISRAEL.` · `TERSE, WITH UNFINISHED EDGES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to appreciate one unfinished work. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind something left incomplete: a project you set down, a letter never sent, a garden half planted, maybe something someone you love began and didn't finish. Don't fix it. Don't judge it. Look at what is there, the way students read the Yerushalmi: as something worth learning from exactly as it is. What does the unfinished part tell you that a polished version wouldn't? If you pray, you can give thanks for work that was begun. The bell holds the time.
Yerushalmi. The Jewish sages' name for what's usually called the Jerusalem Talmud, though its sages taught in the Galilee, not Jerusalem itself. Today's word.
Your line: the land's talmud. Today, step outside after sunset and count the first stars you can see, one, two, three. Day nine hundred eight.

howItsDone: The Jerusalem Talmud is studied in yeshivas and by individuals alongside the Babylonian Talmud, and is turned to especially for the farming laws of the land of Israel.

fork.setup: you're a student outside at dusk, trying to know whether it's night yet. you see two stars. what do you say?
fork.reveal: one star is day, three are night, and two leave it in doubt. the sages turned an abstract rule into something you can see.

original.note: Hebrew: the Jerusalem Talmud, though its sages taught in the Galilee.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Talmud written in Jerusalem.
what it means: the Talmud of the Land of Israel, made by sages in the Galilee, discussing the Mishnah.
what a scholar hears: its older names, the Talmud of the Land of Israel and of the West, say where it came from better than Jerusalem does.
recall: a town for the sages to keep teaching

notes: Index hook ('around 400 CE') had a date; per the claims rule the script's hook line drops it. No date is stated in the voice.
Star rule (one star day, two doubtful, three night) paraphrased from Yerushalmi Berakhot 1:1 (also Bavli Shabbat 35b). Confirm location.
Galilee sages (Tiberias, Sepphoris, Caesarea) and older names 'Talmud of the Land of Israel' / 'Talmud of the West' (Talmuda de-Eretz Yisrael, Talmud Ma'arava): confirm phrasing.
'Some readers sense a work never fully smoothed out' is hedged; scholars debate whether the Yerushalmi was left unedited. Confirm framing.
Language described as 'close to the Aramaic spoken around them' (Galilean/Western Aramaic); confirm.
